summary: Defines an extension to the IPv6 multicast addressing architecture in which a multicast address is built from a network's unicast prefix. A network that receives a unicast prefix automatically gets its own multicast addresses, without needing an inter-domain allocation protocol. It was later updated by RFCs 3956, 4489 and 7371.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3306 defines an IPv6 multicast address format that includes the unicast prefix of the network that owns the address. This lets network operators identify multicast addresses from their assigned unicast prefix without running an inter-domain allocation protocol.

subtitle: How an IPv6 multicast address can include the unicast prefix of the network that owns it.

tldr.problem: IPv6 multicast addressing has no built-in method for dynamic address allocation. The existing IPv4 allocation approach uses several protocols.
tldr.mechanism: The address format includes the owning network's unicast prefix and its prefix length. A flag marks prefix-based addresses, allowing a domain with a unicast prefix to identify multicast addresses tied to it.
tldr.outcome: The format avoids a need to run an inter-domain multicast allocation protocol. RFC 3306 was updated by RFC 3956, RFC 4489, and RFC 7371.

today: RFC 3306 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3956, RFC 4489, and RFC 7371. Read those updates with this document.

sections.title: The Multicast Allocation Problem
sections.content:
The IPv6 addressing architecture described in RFC 2373 has no built-in support for dynamically allocating multicast addresses. RFC 3306 adds encoded information to multicast addresses so IPv6 multicast and source-specific multicast addresses can be allocated dynamically.

The RFC aims to reduce the number of protocols needed for dynamic allocation. It says unicast-prefix-based allocation removes, at a minimum, the need to run the Multicast Address Allocation Protocol and the Multicast Address-Set Claim protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 did not include a built-in way to assign multicast group addresses dynamically. This RFC puts the network's prefix into the group address so operators can identify addresses associated with their network.

sections.title: Fields in the Multicast Address
sections.content:
The format keeps the IPv6 multicast marker, flags, and scope, then uses an 8-bit reserved field, an 8-bit plen, a 64-bit network-prefix field, and a 32-bit group ID. The four flag bits are 0 0 P T. P says whether the address is based on a unicast prefix; when P is 1, T MUST also be 1.

The reserved field MUST be zero. plen gives the number of prefix bits that identify the subnet. The network-prefix field holds the unicast prefix of the domain that owns or allocates the multicast address; its non-significant bits SHOULD be zero. The address scope MUST NOT exceed the scope of the embedded prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The address has fields for the multicast marker, scope, prefix length, network prefix, and group ID. Its prefix flag marks the address as based on a unicast prefix, and the address scope cannot be broader than that prefix's scope.

sections.title: How Long the Address Remains Valid
sections.content:
The lifetime of a unicast-prefix-based multicast address SHOULD NOT exceed the Valid Lifetime for its unicast prefix in the Neighbor Discovery Router Advertisement. The lifetime supports the Abstract API for Multicast Address Allocation.

The Valid Lifetime value does not itself mean that the prefix expires when the value runs out. The RFC says the value is typically constant until renumbering is scheduled; after that, the prefix does become invalid. Continuing to use multicast addresses after their prefix becomes invalid may cause operational problems, including packet discard by routers that perform prefix policy checks.
sections.plainLanguage: A multicast address should not outlast the validity period advertised for its unicast prefix. If the network prefix becomes invalid after renumbering, continued use of the old multicast address can cause problems.

sections.title: Source-Specific Multicast and Examples
sections.content:
To form a source-specific multicast address, a node MUST set P to 1, plen to 0, and the network-prefix field to 0. This produces the range FF3x::/32, where x is any valid scope. The source address in the IPv6 header identifies the owner of the multicast address.

The RFC gives an example: the unicast prefix 3FFE:FFFF:1::/48 corresponds to the multicast prefix FF3x:0030:3FFE:FFFF:0001::/96. It also says IPv6 SSM multicast addresses have the format FF3x::/96.
sections.plainLanguage: For source-specific multicast, the prefix length and network-prefix fields are zero while the prefix flag is set. The RFC's example shows how a network prefix appears within a multicast prefix.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The embedded unicast prefix can help identify the allocation domain for a multicast address. However, an allocation domain can avoid being traced by using a prefix that was not assigned to it or by embedding a prefix with a smaller scope.

Source-specific multicast can sometimes help prevent denial-of-service attacks from arbitrary sources, but the RFC makes no guarantee. It points to the source-specific multicast architecture for more detailed security discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: The embedded prefix can indicate which domain allocated an address, but it is not proof of ownership. Source-specific multicast can help against some denial-of-service attacks, though it does not guarantee protection.
